subjects.name: Human-Centred Design
subjects.description: Understand student needs through interviews, observation and iterative prototyping. This semester I am designing a campus study-space finder. Weekly work includes research ethics, interview synthesis, accessibility and usability evaluation. I want to make recommendations traceable to participant evidence rather than my own assumptions.

subjects.name: Applied Data Analytics
subjects.description: Use Python and statistical reasoning to clean, explore and communicate data. The current project examines transport delays using an anonymised classroom dataset. Assessment rewards reproducible analysis, justified assumptions, clear charts and honest discussion of uncertainty.

subjects.name: Software Engineering Practice
subjects.description: Develop and evaluate software in a small team using user stories, version control, automated tests and sprint retrospectives. Our project is a library study-room booking service. I am responsible for booking validation and the test plan, while rotating code-review duties with teammates.

assignments.title: Campus study spaces: research report
assignments.brief: Write a 1,500-word research report investigating how commuting students find suitable campus study spaces. Conduct three consented interviews, describe recruitment and limitations, identify three evidence-backed themes and translate them into design requirements. Include an anonymised interview guide and a theme-to-evidence table. Assessment: research process 25%, evidence and synthesis 35%, actionable requirements 25%, communication and ethics 15%. Do not treat three interviews as representative of the whole student body.
assignments.tutorFeedback: Your themes are clearly organised and your ethical handling of interview notes is appropriate. The limitations paragraph correctly acknowledges the small sample. Strengthen the connection between each requirement and the underlying interview evidence: the power-access requirement needs a specific anonymised example. Separate what participants said from what you inferred. The recommendation to display availability is promising, but explain how stale data could mislead students.
assignments.reflection: I finished the coding a day before submission and rushed the requirements table. I am pleased that I stated the sample limitation rather than claiming all students want the same features. Before the prototype, I will map each requirement to at least one observation and label assumptions explicitly.
assignments.submittedWork: I interviewed three commuting students about finding somewhere to study between classes. All described a decision between quiet, power access and proximity to their next class. One participant checks two floors before finding a free desk; another prefers a familiar location even when it is noisy. I coded the notes using access, uncertainty and comfort, then grouped repeated observations. The first theme is uncertainty: students cannot know whether a space meets their needs until they arrive. The second is time pressure between classes. The third is the trade-off between quiet space and reliable charging. I propose filters for noise and power, clear opening hours, and an indication of when availability information was last updated. This evidence supports exploring those features; it does not establish their priority across campus. Recruitment through classmates and the small sample limit generalisation. Next, I would include students with accessibility requirements and compare weekday and evening use.
assignments.approach: I used a semi-structured interview guide, consolidated notes after each interview and colour-coded repeated observations. I drafted the limitations section before the recommendations to keep my claims proportional to the evidence.
assignments.challenges: The difficult part was distinguishing a participant preference from a broader design requirement. I also underestimated the time needed to organise quotations and consent notes.
assignments.collaboration: I conducted the work individually. A classmate checked whether the interview questions were leading but did not provide research data or write any section.
assignments.rubric: I checked the ethics and communication criteria, but the evidence-to-requirement links needed another pass. My next revision will add a traceability table and explain the risk of outdated availability information.

assignments.title: Transport delays: exploratory analysis
assignments.brief: Analyse the provided 240-row transport-delay dataset in a reproducible Python notebook. Explain missing values, compare delay distributions across routes, include at least three labelled charts and discuss uncertainty. Submit a 1,000-word report and the notebook. Do not claim that an observed association proves causation. Criteria: cleaning and reproducibility 30%, statistical reasoning 35%, visual communication 20%, limitations 15%.
assignments.tutorFeedback: The notebook runs from top to bottom and the missing-value decision is transparent. Your box plot is useful, but state the units in every axis label. You correctly avoid a causal claim in the discussion; use the same cautious wording in the executive summary. Add route-level sample counts so readers can judge how much evidence supports each comparison.
assignments.reflection: I initially wrote that passenger load causes delays, then changed the discussion after reviewing confounding. I missed the same wording in the summary. A final consistency pass should check every headline against the actual analysis, not just spelling.
assignments.submittedWork: I checked route identifiers, duplicate records and timestamp formats before calculating delay minutes. Twelve records had no arrival time. I reported those records separately and excluded them from delay calculations, leaving 228 observations. Route C had a median delay of eight minutes and a longer upper tail than Routes A and B. The box plot communicates the spread more clearly than comparing means alone. A scatter plot showed greater delay on some high-passenger trips, but time of day and route length may confound that pattern. The dataset covers one teaching week, so it cannot establish a long-term reliability ranking. The notebook includes the cleaning steps and counts after each transformation. I recommend collecting several more weeks and adding weather and incident fields before drawing operational conclusions.
assignments.approach: I wrote the cleaning pipeline first, recorded row counts and used descriptive statistics to select charts before writing the report.
assignments.challenges: I spent too long styling the charts before checking sample sizes. I need to prioritise analytical correctness over presentation polish.
assignments.collaboration: I worked individually and used the lab discussion to check my understanding of missing-data options. My notebook and interpretations are my own.
assignments.rubric: Reproducibility is strong. To improve statistical reasoning and communication, I will add per-route counts and standardise cautious language and units across all sections.

assignments.title: Study-space finder: interactive prototype
assignments.brief: Build an interactive mobile prototype from the research findings. Demonstrate finding a quiet space with charging access, checking opening hours and recovering from no results. Conduct three task-based usability sessions. Submit the prototype link, an 800-word rationale and an evaluation summary. Assess evidence-based decisions, navigation, accessibility and iteration. Record each team member contribution.
assignments.tutorFeedback: Formative studio feedback: the no-results recovery is helpful. Before testing, use neutral task instructions and avoid telling participants which filter to select. Keep the last-updated label prominent so availability is not mistaken for a live guarantee.
assignments.reflection: I want to test whether students understand the freshness label without explaining it first. Our team has agreed to fix high-impact navigation problems before adding animation.
assignments.submittedWork: Our prototype starts with a location list and optional filters for quiet areas and charging access. Each location card shows opening hours and a clearly labelled last-updated time. The no-results screen offers to remove one filter rather than leaving the student at a dead end. I am drafting the evaluation tasks: find a suitable space before a 2 pm class, check whether it is open, and recover when no charging locations are available. We will record task completion, wrong turns and comments without treating a three-person evaluation as statistically conclusive. The current prototype uses larger tap targets and text labels alongside icons. Outstanding work includes contrast checks and a clearer explanation of estimated availability.
assignments.approach: I converted the research requirements into three user tasks, sketched the empty and error states, and used the rubric to prioritise screens.
assignments.challenges: It is tempting to add features that were never supported by the research. Coordinating interview times around commuting schedules is also difficult.
assignments.collaboration: I own task scripts and accessibility checks. Priya builds the location detail screens; Sam manages the interactive links. We review each other’s work on Tuesday and Thursday and record decisions in shared notes.
assignments.rubric: Each design decision will cite a research observation. The evaluation summary will distinguish observed usability problems from suggested features. I still need to test text resizing and keyboard focus.

assignments.title: Room booking service: implementation and test portfolio
assignments.brief: Deliver a room-booking service with create, view and cancel booking flows. Prevent overlapping bookings and invalid times. Include automated unit and integration tests, a README with setup instructions and a 1,200-word test portfolio. Evaluate both valid requests and attempts that should be rejected. Explain limitations and provide reproducible evidence rather than claiming complete coverage.
assignments.reflection: I realised that a passing happy-path test says little about conflict handling. I now write one rejection case next to each acceptance case. The concurrency behaviour needs an explicit test rather than assuming the database will handle it.
assignments.submittedWork: I have implemented validation for start time before end time, supported room identifiers and conflicts with existing reservations. A request from 10:00 to 11:00 is allowed when the room is free; an overlapping request from 10:30 to 11:30 is rejected. Adjacent reservations ending and starting at 11:00 are permitted. Cancelling a booking releases the slot. The test plan includes empty input, unknown rooms, reversed times, duplicate submission and cancellation of a missing booking. Remaining work is testing simultaneous requests so two callers cannot reserve the same slot before either write completes. The portfolio will include the expected result, actual result and evidence for each scenario.
assignments.approach: I turned each user story into a contract, listed boundary conditions and wrote tests before extending the validation code.
assignments.challenges: The hardest boundary is whether an end time equal to another start time counts as a conflict. We documented the half-open interval rule so implementation and tests agree.
assignments.collaboration: I own validation and tests. Aisha owns the persistence adapter and Liam the client interface. We pair-review changes affecting shared request types and require reproducible bug steps.
assignments.rubric: I have evidence for normal and invalid booking flows. Before submission I need an integration run, a concurrency test and a clean-machine README check.

assignments.title: Professional practice: individual reflection
assignments.brief: Write a 1,200-word individual reflection on a significant challenge during the team project. Describe the situation, analyse your decisions using a reflective framework, support claims with project evidence and propose a specific development plan. Avoid simply narrating events or assigning blame. Criteria: critical analysis 40%, evidence 25%, actionable development 25%, presentation 10%.
assignments.reflection: I have a clear incident but need to move beyond describing it. I will explain how my assumption affected the team and identify a practical habit I can test in the next sprint.
assignments.submittedWork: Working outline: I will examine our disagreement about overlap validation. Initially I assumed that adjacent bookings should be rejected to leave a cleaning buffer, while the documented requirement allowed them. I want to analyse why I treated an unstated assumption as a requirement and how a shared example clarified the disagreement. Evidence will include the original issue, the boundary-case table and the revised tests. My development plan is to write acceptance examples before implementation and explicitly separate business rules from personal preferences. I still need to connect the discussion to the reflective framework and explain what I would do differently in another team.
assignments.approach: I am collecting dated project artefacts and outlining situation, interpretation, alternatives and next steps before writing paragraphs.
assignments.challenges: I find it easier to explain a technical fix than critically examine my own decision-making. I need to keep the reflection constructive and evidence-based.
assignments.collaboration: This is an individual submission. I will check factual details with teammates and anonymise their comments rather than attributing motives.
assignments.rubric: The draft plan addresses evidence and action. The largest gap is critical analysis: compare at least two possible responses and explain why the chosen approach was appropriate.

goals.title: Before the 18 November prototype review, link every design requirement to an anonymised interview observation and identify any remaining assumptions.
Add route sample counts and minute units to all transport charts, then check that the executive summary makes no causal claim unsupported by the analysis.
By 20 November, write paired acceptance and rejection tests for booking overlap, invalid times, duplicate requests and cancellation, including one concurrency case.
Run three neutral usability sessions before 16 November and record task completion, navigation mistakes and whether participants understand the availability timestamp.
Plan study blocks every Sunday: reserve two focused sessions per subject, leave one catch-up block, and review actual progress on Friday without sacrificing sleep.
